article.title: Women Politicians Under Attack
article.author: Steven Hill
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Bernadet Greene-Placentia, the Democratic candidate for Arizona’s 8th Congressional District, claimed a week ago that she was struck in the head, knocked unconscious and raped by two men while she was repairing one of her campaign signs. Greene-Placentia, who is no shrinking violet having worked as a long-haul trucker and small business owner, filed an official incident report with the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office (MCSO), but didn’t do so until 17 days after the alleged event occurred. Due to that delay, some are doubting her story , calling it a publicity stunt to boost her campaign in a Republican-leaning district. But according to the police report, Greene-Placentia sustained several documented injuries, including a bump on her head , finger-type bruising on her arms, and bruises on her flank. She told investigators that one of the men said “Democratic bitch” at some point during the attack. She has explained that her reasons for not immediately reporting to the police or undergoing a sexual assault medical forensic exam was due to her trauma, shock, embarrassment and self-shaming, and not wanting the incident to distract from her campaign. She says she just wanted to “bury it.” So the debate rages, even as the sheriff’s office continues to investigate, with no suspects so far publicly identified or charged. However this case turns out, the truth is, Bernadet Greene-Placentia is not the only woman candidate or politician who has reported claims of physical violence, harassment and/or intimidation. Her story is yet another example illustrating a disturbing and broader pattern: over the last several years, a national and even global backlash against women’s political rise has been rearing its ugly head. Women elected officials are being intimidated, harassed and threatened in growing and alarming numbers. And authoritarian leaders like Donald Trump, Argentina’s Javier Milei and Brazil’s jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro have led the way in fomenting this hostile climate, using digital media and public statements as primary weapons in their arsenal. Related: Why Are Democrats Shooting Themselves in the Foot on Ranked Choice Voting? Reality rearing its ugly head A study by the Brennan Center found that women holding state and local office in the US were three to four times as likely as men to experience gender-based abuse; and women state legislators were nearly four times as likely as men to experience abuse of a sexual nature. Moreover, women as well as people of color legislators reported experiencing more severe and threatening forms of abuse than their male or white respondents. In interviews, one female state legislator related her experience of strangers “identifying my address or talking about my daughter or my mom or, you know, making overt rape or death threats. . . . My husband just showed me a thread on Reddit yesterday about people talking about — men — what they would do to me. And we women just sort of have to compartmentalize it.” Another female legislator said of her harassers, “They don’t directly say, ‘I’m going to kill her children.’ But they’ll make comments like, ‘We’re going to take over her home. Here’s the address. Here’s a photo of it. She lives here in [town], but her kids don’t go to school [in town] — they go in [neighboring town].’” A female state representative from Texas, said, “Sometimes we’re on the legislative ﬂoor, and in the galleries above us there are people who are armed. And especially when we’re having those controversial debates, I’m thinking, ‘God, one person. It just takes one person.’ We’re like sitting ducks. I’m still going to do what I’m going to do as far as legislating. But I’m not naive enough to think it could never happen to us.” In the past, high profile attacks against women leaders have set the nation on edge. In June 2025, a gunman assassinated former Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband. Who can forget the brutal shooting and near-murder of Congresswoman Gabby Giffords outside a supermarket where the congresswoman was meeting with constituents in Tucson AZ. Or the attempted kidnapping of Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer in 2020, and the hammer attack on Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s husband by a right-wing zealot looking for the Speaker in her San Francisco home. Male political leaders have also been targeted for political violence, including President Donald Trump and right-wing activist Charlie Kirk. Yet evidence shows that women politicians face unique and pervasive harms. In one national safety survey, 93% of women legislator respondents reported experiencing some form of abuse or harassment as legislators. Harm often manifests on a day-to-day basis as sexualized threats , professional dismissal or appearance-based insults. Not surprisingly, women in ofﬁce, and especially women of color, report having to take extra time and adopt special tactics to stay safe. Women state legislators are nearly twice as likely as men to change their travel routes because of abuse concerns, and more than six times as likely as men to avoid traveling alone. Fifty-ﬁve percent of women of color legislators said they avoid traveling alone. And nearly half of women officeholders said they were less willing to run for reelection or higher office because of the shocking levels of threats and abuse. This is serious, Taliban-like stuff. Another study found that female mayors are more likely than men to experience physical violence, harassment and psychological abuse, and those who suffered physical violence were more likely to have considered ending their political careers. A separate study by the same researchers concluded that women state senators with higher levels of power (party or committee leaders) were more likely than other women to experience psychological abuse and sexualized abuse and violence; Democratic women state senators faced more sexualized abuse and violence than Republican women. Another study found that, among congressional candidates, women of color were most likely to experience sexist, racist and violent abuse online. Related: From “11,780 Votes” to Trump’s 2026 Election Power Grab The role of digital media in attacks on women leaders An important and often overlooked component of the backlash is the way that the internet and digital media platforms have turbocharged these harms. These increasingly dominant communication tools are providing a global platform to bad actors intent on doing bad things to their targeted victims. This is much more than simply the continuation of sexism by other means. These are potent communication technologies that have unleashed the worst impulses of the worst specimens of humanity, and allowed them to find each other anywhere in the world, and encourage, strategize and share tactics together. Male extremist groups like the Proud Boys and Boogaloo Bois right-wing militias congregate in clandestine Facebook Groups that can be walled off as “hidden” or secret and accessible only to admitted members. Other secret meet-ups on the internet can be found on platforms like subReddits, Parler, Signal, Telegram, WhatsApp, and chat rooms on 4chan and 8kun. Some of these are encrypted against unauthorized entry into private groups, including by law enforcement. In their digital lairs, participants have circulated links to manuals on bomb construction, kidnapping, making flash stun grenades , snipers, and murder. Some of these groups have had thousands of members . In years past, if you were the only person in your geographic area who had extremist views, organizing with other like-minded but geographically dispersed extremists was costly and logistically difficult. Now, the use of digital media drastically reduces these costs and allows such individuals to find each other more easily to organize and collaborate. These online forums – kind of like hidden “digital hideouts” - are filled with men of all ages concealed behind the anonymity of the internet. Inside their digital Fight Club of fury they can easily direct their bitter hostility at their chosen targets of women in general, and female elected leaders in particular. These “het-bro” digital hideouts are now increasingly accompanied by other technologies, such as self-learning artificial intelligence and highly realistic immersive technologies, resulting in a proliferation in the production of deepfakes, the vast majority of which are imitative pornography videos featuring the likenesses of real women. Fake nude images have spread all over the internet, increasing by 290 percent in recent years. Linda Robinson, a senior fellow for Women and Foreign Policy at the Council on Foreign Relations, says “The radicalization of politics on the right and the power of toxic tech are reinforcing and accelerating long-standing gender bias rather than breaking it down.” This is a double blow: the liberatory qualities and euphoria of the early years of the internet are being strangled by the refusal of tech companies to take responsibility or liability for the harms of their technologies-on-steroids. At the same time, governments have failed to mount effective regulation. Related: AI Warfare Goes Unchecked Male populists lead the backlash The targeting of women political leaders by far-right extremists and elected autocratic populists, both online and offline, shouldn’t come as a surprise in the Trump/ Milei/Bolsonaro/Putin/Modi era. Though I confess that I had thought the US was further along in its egalitarian development. However, the rise of Donald Trump shows otherwise. Trump has gleefully fed this backlash with his constant denigration of female politicians and journalists ( here and here ). Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired, forced out, or blocked promotion of a number of high-ranking female military officers, including the chief of Naval Operations, the US military’s representative to NATO and the Coast Guard commandant (he also has dismissed numerous racial minority leaders in the military). These and other right-wing leaders’ constant anti-women jabbering has had the effect of normalizing such attacks: “Boys will be boys, what can you do?” And this is not just a US phenomenon. Around the world, almost half of women legislators have received violent threats and are much more likely to be targeted for their gender than are men, according to the Inter-Parliamentary Union , an international organization of national parliaments. The study found that sexism, harassment and violence against women parliamentarians are very real and pervasive, and exists to different degrees in every country. The IPU report shows a shocking list of harmful and dangerous behaviors directed at female parliamentarians, stretching out along a malicious continuum of abuse: 66% were subject to humiliating sexual or sexist remarks; 42% had humiliating or sexually charged images of themselves spread through digital media; 44% were subjected to threats of death, rape, beatings or abduction; 33% were the victims of harassment in the form of insistent and uninvited behavior or verbal contact that some of the targets found frightening; 26% were subjected to one or more acts of physical violence, and 22% were subjected to one or more acts of sexual violence. That’s shocking: over one fifth of female legislators were subjected to sexual violence. How can a woman legislator focus on doing her job when she is immersed in such a hostile work environment? And when she is hearing constant stories from her female colleagues of their own abuse and mistreatment? The fact that they continue in the face of this persistent male bellicosity and posturing shows an astounding amount of courage. The rising popularity of right-wing political leaders around the world poses a threat to women and democracy, says Robinson from the Council on Foreign Relations. “Populist politicians explicitly attack feminism and gender equality or cloak their regressive stands behind the rhetoric of restoring ‘traditional family values. ’” And they increasingly make gender-based appeals to win votes, including to young men and men of color . Related: Centi-Billionaires Dominating US Media and Politics Threaten Democracy Women’s slow leakage of political power This ongoing demeaning of women by the world’s most powerful male leaders is setting an example that is reversing women’s political gains over the past 20 years. And given the hostile treatment and environment, women are shying away from political office because of this onslaught of violent threats and online abuse. Consequently, women today occupy only 27.5 percent of the world’s legislative seats (about the same as the US , at 28%), even as the number of women leading their countries’ governments has sharply declined. The number of countries (out of 195) with women serving as a head of state or government has fallen from a high of 38 in 2023 to 28 today . High profile female heads-of-state in New Zealand, Finland, Slovakia, Scotland and the Netherlands have resigned or chosen not to run for reelection due to the harassing environment. According to the Center for American Women and Politics , the number of Republican women candidates has declined dramatically , by 28%, since 2022, and the number of women nominees for both Democrats and Republicans has declined. Trump’s regal restoration has been part of a global backlash against women’s political rise. This reactionary rebound has all the hallmarks of a winner-take-all, zero sum game: a perception by many that, for women to win , men must lose . These are very worrisome trends. The battle is on, and its signs have been hiding in plain sight as part of an ongoing assault against the decades-long effort to build a more egalitarian, democratic society. DemocracySOS
